## The number that isn't a number

Seven supplier invoices, exported from the ERP into the **Model** sheet. Amount column in euros,
column B. At a glance it looks like a normal table: seven figures, one below the other.

It isn't. An export brings the source system's defects into Excel too: a figure that arrives
already as text — with the thousands separator typed inside the raw value (`12,500`) or with an
invisible trailing character — stays **text**, not a number. There's no red hash to flag it: the only clue is
the cell's alignment. Real numbers align right. Text aligns left.
Look at column B before writing any formula.

The amounts generated range from about {p0} to {p1}.
Some of these figures — we won't tell you which, that's the point of the audit — are text disguised as numbers.

**SUM** and **COUNT** share the same rule: they count only what is really a number.
Text they skip, silently. The total you'll get in B12 is the REAL one, not the one you'd
expect by adding up the seven figures by eye.

In B13 you'll find **COUNTA** already calculated on the same column: it counts every non-empty cell, text
included. It's up to you, in B14, to compute **COUNT**: how many of those seven cells are real numbers.
The difference between B13 and B14 is the hard proof of how many invoices are missing from the total.
M0D-02-TESTOCOMENUMERO.22: Look at the alignment in column B: text cells move left, real numbers stay right. It's the only visible clue.
M0D-02-TESTOCOMENUMERO.23: =SUM(B4:B10). Text cells stay out of the total without any error: that's normal, it's the phenomenon you're observing.
M0D-02-TESTOCOMENUMERO.24: =COUNT(B4:B10) counts only real numbers. COUNTA(B4:B10), already in B13, counts text too: compare the two values to see how many cells are dirty.
M0D-02-TESTOCOMENUMERO.title: The number that isn't a number

## Raw data: two ways an export lies to you

You've pasted the CRM's supplier invoice export into the sheet: {p0} rows.
Before adding anything up, data pasted from outside must always be checked: two
problems are so common that Excel built two dedicated commands around them (Data >
**Text to Columns**, Data > **Remove Duplicates**), which this build doesn't have yet.
You train them anyway, by hand, understanding what they really do:

- **Text to Columns** takes a column where several pieces of information ended up pasted
  into a single block of text, separated by a character (comma, semicolon, space),
  and splits them into separate columns. Look at B{p1}, below: that's how
  raw data arrives from many CRMs, name and amount stuck together with a `;`. In real
  Excel you'd select the column, open Text to Columns, choose "delimited" and
  the semicolon, and get two clean columns.
- **Remove Duplicates** compares the rows of a selection and deletes exact copies,
  keeping just one. There's one below: a supplier appears twice, same name
  and same amount ({p2}) — it's not a customer who invoiced twice,
  it's the same row pasted twice by mistake.

The problem isn't cosmetic: that duplicate **inflates the total**. If you add it up as it is,
you get {p3}; the real total, with that supplier counted only once, is
{p4}. The difference — {p5} — is a number that would end up
in a fairness opinion or a working capital adjustment without anyone noticing.

Find the duplicate, then fix the total without deleting anything: it's the habit to
have when you work on a file you didn't prepare, and you don't know yet whom to trust.

## A wrong number doesn't always shout

So far an error in a sheet has always been visible: a red hash, `#DIV/0!`, `#REF!`.
What follows is more dangerous because you can't see it at all.

Below are three divisions of the same group, in the **{settore}** sector. For each one column
**D** already calculates the EBITDA margin: revenue minus costs, divided by revenue. The formulas are written
and locked — you don't have to edit them — and none of the three returns an error.

One of them, though, is wrong. Not in the sign, not in the subtraction: in the **denominator**. Instead of
dividing by revenue, it divides by costs. The difference between "column B" and "column C" is a
single letter, and the number that comes out isn't absurd: it's a plausible EBITDA margin, the
same order of magnitude as the other two. No glance-test tells it apart from the real numbers:
you have to reread the formula, not trust what it shows.

Find it, recompute by hand the correct margin for that division, and write it where indicated.

## Tracing the chain without recalculating

A quick valuation model, already built by someone else. Revenue {p0},
expected growth {p1}, EBITDA margin {p2}: from these three numbers
the sheet already derives projected revenue (B4) and projected EBITDA (B6). They're real
formulas, locked: your job isn't to rewrite them, it's to understand what they hold without
recalculating everything in your head.

**Ctrl+[** (Trace precedents), pressed on a cell, moves the selection to the cells that
formula depends on DIRECTLY. Go up to B6 and press Ctrl+[: the selection jumps to
B4 and B5, the two ingredients of EBITDA. Press it again on B4 and you jump to B2 and B3. That's how
you trace a chain in a few seconds instead of guessing. **Ctrl+]** (Trace dependents)
does the reverse: from an input, it shows everything that uses it.

Net debt is {p3} (B7), the reference multiple is {p4}
(B8). In B9 build the final number: enterprise value minus debt.

Then comes the really useful part: in B11 we ask you for the enterprise value alone, that is
a piece INSIDE B9's formula that has no cell of its own. Redoing the multiplication
is one way to find it. The professional way is different: enter edit mode on B9 with
**F2**, select with the mouse (or Shift+arrows) the piece `B6*B8` inside the formula
bar, and press **F9**. Excel replaces it there, in place of the selection, with its
calculated value — without leaving the cell, without touching anything else. Read the number and
press **ESC**, not Enter: Enter would paste that value in place of the fragment and the
formula would stop being a formula.

M0D-06-GUARDZERO.17:
## A guard, not a plaster

**{magazzino}** reports its operating cost and orders fulfilled for the last four quarters.
The first quarter cost {p1} for {p2} orders fulfilled — the cost
per order is that ratio, and it's the number that says whether logistics can handle the volume going through.

In quarter **{p3}**, though, the warehouse was shut ({motivo}): zero orders fulfilled,
but rent and staff — {p5} — were paid anyway. Dividing that
cost by zero orders produces `#DIV/0!`. It's not a typo: in that quarter
the "cost per order" simply doesn't exist. No number, however reasonable, represents it.

**`IFERROR(formula, value_if_error)`** catches the error and replaces it with something you
chose. In M0-B you already saw a case where the fallback was a defensible numeric estimate (a
list price). Here there's no equivalent: the right fallback is the text `"n/a"`, which tells the
truth — the figure isn't there — instead of a zero or an invented number that would end up
in a total anyway.

The part that really matters: **write the formula only once**, in B6, and copy it across the whole row
B6:E6. You already know, as you write it, that one of the four quarters has a zero denominator — so the
guard isn't an add-on for the rare case, it's part of the base formula from the first quarter.
In M0-B you learned not to put IFERROR everywhere out of habit; here, if even one quarter
of the row can have zero in the denominator, the guard must be in ALL the cells, because it's one
formula, not four independent ones.

A craft note, on the side: when a table grows beyond the screen, the row labels and
the period headers disappear as you scroll. In Excel you lock them from View -> Freeze
Panes (legacy sequence: **Alt, W, F**). It isn't checked here — it doesn't show in the values — but the
sheet for this level already comes with the label column and the header frozen,
so you see the effect while you work, before you ever have to set it yourself.
